context.hint: A patched copy of the Node.js HTTP client now forces every tested caller-supplied path back onto the supplied origin while preserving literal path text; the vulnerable copy still delivered thirteen of twenty-seven cases to a second loopback server. Method, body, query, same-origin double-slash and dot-segment behavior matched between copies. Permissions: run both copies, bind loopback servers, call the public entry points, and inspect error types and messages. The next question is whether the repair is over-broad or fragile: do public validation expectations still hold, and do unusual origin forms (hostname versus loopback address spelling, uppercase or cross-scheme absolute paths, a bare scheme prefix, bracketed IPv6) stay contained without throwing?
context.surface: Dependency-free Node.js HTTP/1.1 client; public dispatcher accepting an origin plus a path or pathname option; internal URL parser with a plain-object branch and a separate string-path branch; disposable loopback origin and target servers that log request line, Host header and body; library diagnostics channel that exposes the resolved origin and path for each outgoing request.
assumptions: A Node.js runtime is available and the library imports directly from an editable working copy with no installed runtime dependencies.
The observer may read the source, edit two resolution sites in a separate patched copy, and run ordinary HTTP calls.
The attacker controls only the path or pathname string; the application fixes the origin URL and method, and follows no attacker-controlled redirect logic in this scenario.
Disposable HTTP servers can bind ephemeral loopback ports on the loopback interface; one server acts as the fixed origin and a second as the foreign target, and both record every request.
No public target is contacted. The official benchmark verdict is produced externally from an exported patch, so local fixtures and matrices are supporting evidence only.

incumbent.text: Wire-first reproduction then containment repair: stand up two disposable loopback servers (origin and target) that log method, request URL, Host and body; prove the foreign delivery end to end for both public input forms and a widened spelling set; add an origin-containment rule at both resolution sites so the supplied text is resolved literally under the supplied origin; then run a differential keep/reach matrix on vulnerable and patched copies plus a clean-apply check on a pristine tree.

candidates.text: Hypothesis: comparing serialized origin strings can fire on a base origin spelled with a hostname while the absolute path names the loopback address on the same socket, and the literal rebuild could still land on the foreign spelling if any later step re-resolves absolutely. Prerequisites and permissions: both copies and two servers, one reachable as the hostname and as the loopback address. Bounded test: use a hostname base with a loopback-named path, and the reverse, logging Host and resolved origin at each server. Expected supporting result: the patched copy stays on the base origin string and the vulnerable copy changes origin in at least the hostname-base direction. Falsifier: any target delivery, throw, or later re-resolution to the foreign spelling on the patched copy. Cleanup: stop servers and diff the logs.

Hypothesis: bracketed IPv6 origins break a helper that manipulates host and port strings, causing a throw or a fall-through for protocol-relative and absolute IPv6 paths. Prerequisites and permissions: patched and vulnerable copies; if ::1 cannot bind, permission to call the resolution helper directly. Bounded test: bind fixture servers on ::1 when available; otherwise feed bracketed origins and paths through the helper and assert resolved-origin equality. Expected supporting result: every bracketed spelling stays on the base IPv6 origin with literal path text. Falsifier: a non-origin origin, an exception on brackets, or a crash. Cleanup: close sockets and keep the logical table.

Hypothesis (over-breadth counterexample): rejecting every path that begins with two slashes is a simpler repair that would pass leak tests but break same-origin double-slash and same-origin absolute-URL controls, silently changing the accepted public contract. Prerequisites and permissions: both copies, loopback servers, and permission to run identical controls. Bounded test: run ordinary, query, dot-segment, encoded, same-origin double-slash and same-origin absolute controls through both copies and replicate the package's documented path-validation expectations manually. Expected supporting result: controls are unchanged by the containment repair and the documented error strings are identical. Falsifier: any control changed between copies or any validation string changed. Cleanup: reset scratch trees and keep the comparison report.

Hypothesis: a case-varied absolute scheme and a bare scheme prefix exercise protocol normalization differently, so a string comparison could miss them even though ordinary resolution leaks the uppercase form. Prerequisites and permissions: both copies, loopback servers, and permission to call the public entry points. Bounded test: send an uppercase-scheme absolute URL and a bare scheme-prefixed path to both copies, recording resolved origin and status; also compare the no-leading-slash error contract. Expected supporting result: the vulnerable copy leaks the uppercase form, while the patched copy contains both and keeps error parity for the no-leading-slash case. Falsifier: a patched target delivery or a divergent error type or message. Cleanup: stop servers and release ports.

Hypothesis: an https-scheme absolute path against an http base origin is a foreign origin even though the schemes differ, and must be literalized rather than merged into the http socket address space. Prerequisites and permissions: patched copy, loopback servers, and permission to export and apply a patch. Bounded test: send an absolute URL with the https scheme and a host:port as the path against an http base and record the destination and literal path; separately apply the exported diff to a pristine tree and replay the matrix there. Expected supporting result: the request reaches the http origin with a leading slash followed by that absolute URL as literal text, and the clean-apply replay matches the working patched copy. Falsifier: a foreign delivery or a replay mismatch. Cleanup: remove the scratch pristine tree.

evaluations.rationale: Selected. The differential matrix is a directly observed, discriminating result, and the incumbent's next step is exactly the remaining contract and unusual-origin verification. The generated vectors sharpen that step but none carried executed evidence at selection time.

Deferred and folded into the executed verification block. The over-broad-repair counterexample is the best discriminator against a lazy reject-all fix, and its manual validation assertions were run on both copies.
Deferred, partly executed. Uppercase and bare-scheme paths were measured and error parity was checked; the candidate is narrower than the combined verification action.

Deferred and executed. The hostname-versus-loopback spelling proved that a same-socket path can still change the parsed origin, which is a useful nuance; its later re-resolution concern did not materialize.
Deferred to the packaging round. Cross-scheme containment was verified, but the clean-apply half belonged to the final closure action.

Deferred and executed logically. Bracketed IPv6 sockets could not bind in the container, so the resolution-level table was used; it showed containment for all bracketed spellings on the patched copy and origin changes on the vulnerable parser.

observation.summary: A ten-case edge-origin block and a six-case public-contract block ran against both copies with loopback servers and the diagnostics channel. On the patched copy every edge case kept the base origin: a hostname base with a loopback-named path, the reverse, an uppercase-scheme absolute URL, an https-scheme absolute URL against an http base, a bare scheme prefix, query-only, empty, root and same-origin double-slash paths. On the vulnerable copy five cases changed origin, including the hostname/loopback mismatch in both directions, the uppercase absolute form, and the https absolute form, which attempted TLS to the foreign origin. The contract block was byte-identical between copies: numeric path and pathname produce the same InvalidArgumentError messages, a double-slash-only path produces the same TypeError, and relative, NUL-bearing and asterisk paths are accepted by both because resolution normalizes them before the request-level validator. Bracketed IPv6 binding failed with address-not-available, so IPv6 was recorded as a limitation at this step.
observation.next_hint: Contract parity and unusual-origin containment hold; the remaining uncertainty is packaging. Export the unified diff, apply it to a freshly extracted pristine snapshot with a check-then-apply workflow, compare hashes with the working patched copy, parse the JSON-lines evaluator bundle exactly as an external consumer would, replay both harnesses on the bundle-patched tree, and add a one-site mutant negative control plus a recomputable manifest.
